EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A major winter storm produced heavy snow and sleet accumulation in southern Indiana January 24-26, 2026. A strong low pressure system moved through the Ohio Valley. The winter storm dropped a swath of heavy snow and sleet totaling 6 to 13 inches across southern Indiana. A frigid airmass moved in following the storm, contributing to enhanced societal impact due to a combination of snow-covered roads and dangerously cold wind chills. The impact of this winter storm was felt for weeks following the event.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy snow and sleet totaling 8 to 11 inches fell across Scott County.

The storm featured strong frontogenetical forcing in the mid-levels of the atmosphere, which led to heavy snowfall rates and banding. A layer of warm air aloft streamed northward through central Kentucky and into far southern Indiana, changing precipitation over to sleet for a short period of time in some counties. The winter storm dropped a swath of heavy snow and sleet totaling 6 to 13 inches across southern Indiana. A frigid airmass moved in following the storm, contributing to enhanced societal impact due to a combination of snow-covered roads and dangerously cold wind chills. The impact of this winter storm was felt for weeks following the event.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A wintry mix changed over to snow as temperatures plunged well below freezing behind an arctic front. This created an icy flash freeze environment under a half inch to two inches of snow.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An arctic cold front moved through with a mixture of sleet and rain changing to a period of snow. Snow accumulations were generally an inch or two at best. However, the cold air rushing in with the front and snow allowed the wet pavement to freeze late morning into the afternoon and early evening. This resulted in reports of slide-offs and accidents across the region, with numerous accidents that briefly closed portions of Interstate 69 in northeast Indiana.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Overall dry conditions that had resulted in Extreme Drought (D3) over north-central Indiana by late 2025 generally expanded and intensified throughout January 2026. While D2 and D3 levels were maintained from the previous month, a significant degradation occurred on the January 6th update, where D3 intensity expanded across the heart of the region. These drought conditions remained entrenched without improvement through the end of the month and continued into at least February 2026.||This status quo included a primary sub-region where D3 conditions expanded to cover the entirety of Howard County and much of Carroll and Delaware counties. Significant expansion of Severe Drought (D2) was also noted, moving to encompass the remainder of Clinton, Hamilton, and Vermillion counties. Meanwhile, D2 intensity was maintained across northern Henry County and northwestern Vigo County, with a small additional expansion into north-central Vigo. In the northeast, Tipton County saw an intensification as D3 pushed into its northern portions, while D3 remained fixed in the far northwestern corner of Randolph County.||Precipitation throughout January for these areas was critically low, with many totals falling between 0.75 and 1.25 inches. Specifically, Carroll, Randolph, and Howard counties saw meager totals of 0.75 to 1.10 inches, which directly triggered the expansion of D3 intensity. Even in areas like Henry County, which received a slightly higher 1.50 to 2.25 inches, the moisture was not enough to warrant improvement. These sustained deficits, often totaling less than 50% of normal monthly rainfall, ensured that the drought not only persisted but worsened across the central Indiana landscape.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Precipitation totaled only around 1.1 inches across the month of January. This maintained D2 conditions across much of Howard county with D3 conditions in the rest. On the January 6th update, D3 expanded to cover the remainder of the county. These drought conditions continued into at least February 2026.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: System snow overspread far northern Indiana during the evening hours of January 18th which was followed by periods of lake effect snow on January 19th behind an arctic front. Storm total snowfall accumulations ranged from 2 to 4 inches across portions of far northern Indiana generally along and north of Interstate 80. Strong winds coupled with the snow and blowing snow produced significant visibility reductions at times and hazardous travel conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Light system snow during the late afternoon and evening of January 18th was followed by bands of lake effect snow.  The combination of west wind gusts of 30 to 40 mph and the snowfall resulted in significant visibility reductions at times due to snow and blowing snow. Storm total snow accumulations were in the 2 to 4 inch range. A report of 3 inches of snow was received in South Bend, IN.  Numerous slide-offs and accidents were reported across the region.  In addition, wind chills dropped to as cold as 20 below during the early morning hours of January 19th extending into early afternoon.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A major winter storm that brought Evansville's 2nd largest snowstorm on record impacted southwest Indiana on the 24th with light to moderate snow developing around midday. After a brief lull overnight, moderate to heavy snow developed with a second wave that continued into the morning hours of the 25th. A brief period of sleet had occurred as above freezing temperatures aloft advected north. Colder air wrapped around on the backside, allowing for precipitation to transition back to all snow before ending during the early evening hours. Between 7 to 14 inches of snow and sleet was observed with the lowest totals occurring in Spencer County, IN where the greatest mixing had fallen. ||Significant travel impacts occurred with snow instantly accumulating on all surfaces due to temperatures only in the upper single digits and teens during the bulk of the event. Emergency dispatchers fielded 653 calls in Vanderburgh County, IN with deputies and firefighters responding to dozens of traffic accidents and medical emergencies. Near Evansville at Boeke and Vogel, a 52 year old woman who was driving under the influence was stuck in the snow with a tire coming off the rim of their car during the early morning hours of the 25th. Gibson County, IN issued an Emergency Declaration in line with the state of Indiana, in addition to a travel warning. Wind gusts around 20 to 25 mph led to blowing and drifting snow that led to travel becoming extremely dangerous. The extreme cold after the event hampered clean-up efforts and made snow removal extremely difficult. Key Impacts: transportation delays, traffic accidents, government closures.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Overall dry conditions that had peaked with widespread Extreme Drought (D3) in early March 2026 generally dissipated or significantly improved throughout the remainder of the month. While the month began with an intensification on March 3rd that expanded D3 across counties like Carroll, Clinton, and Howard, a pattern of heavy rainfall triggered weekly improvements. By the March 31st update, Severe Drought (D2) and Extreme Drought (D3) had been completely removed from nearly all 17 previously affected counties.||This dramatic shift included the total elimination of D2/D3 conditions in a broad sub-region covering Warren, Vermillion, Fountain, Vigo, Parke, Montgomery, Boone, Clinton, Howard, Tipton, Hamilton, Madison, Delaware, Henry, and Randolph counties. By the end of the month, the only remaining vestiges of the winter drought were limited to the northern half of Carroll County and a small sliver of northern Tippecanoe County, which both remained in D2. In the eastern corridor, D3 conditions���which had been steady for months���were systematically trimmed back between March 10th and March 24th before finally being removed.||Precipitation throughout March was exceptionally high for these areas, with totals ranging from 4 to as much as 9 inches. Specifically, western counties like Warren and Fountain saw deluge amounts of 9 inches, while the central corridor from Vigo to Boone received 6 to 8.5 inches, providing the necessary moisture to end the drought status by mid-month. Even in the more stubborn drought areas of the northeast, such as Delaware and Howard counties, monthly totals of 4 to 5.5 inches neared or exceeded double the normal rainfall, finally allowing for the termination of severe drought conditions. The remaining counties in D2 would see improvements out of severe drought in early April.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: D3 conditions at the start of the month for much of the county remained in a steady state before heavy rains began to trim the D3 back down on the March 10th issuance and weekly afterwards through the end of the month. D3 drought ended on the 24th with D2 drought ending on the 31st. Rainfall amounts over the month were as much as 5 to 6.5 inches which allowed for the end of severe drought conditions.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful supercell thunderstorm tracked an EF-3 tornado across northern Newton and northwestern Jasper counties and another EF-1 tornado through northern Jasper County during the evening of March 10th. The EF-3 destroyed a number of homes and caused significant damage to many other homes, businesses, and infrastructure, especially in the town of Lake Village where two fatalities occurred as a result of the storm. Additional severe thunderstorms later in the evening brought one inch hail to northern Lake and Porter counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A destructive EF-3 tornado was nearing the end of its lifecycle upon briefly moving into northwest Jasper County and dissipated shortly thereafter. After forming in Kankakee County and causing EF-3 caliber damage in Kankakee and Newton counties, this tornado crossed into far northwestern Jasper County between W 1100 N Road and W 1200 N Road. Along N 1200 W Road just east of I-65, a continuous corridor of trees was entirely uprooted, a few outbuildings were damaged, and the roof was removed from a house. In the community of Forest City, a continuous corridor of trees was uprooted, and a few residences had shingles removed. The tornado diminished in intensity as it moved northeast toward N 1100 W Road, and then dissipated just south of the intersection of N 1100 W Road and W 1300 N Road. The tornado resulted in three fatalities and around a dozen injuries, though none reported in Jasper County. The damage sustained in Jasper County was found to be on the order of EF-1 strength.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Between the evening of March 3 and the late hours of March 4, 2026, a significant hydrologic event unfolded across central Indiana as a stalled frontal boundary interacted with a highly anomalous moisture profile. Driven by a robust 50-knot low-level jet, precipitable water values surged to nearly 1.30 inches���well above the 90th percentile for early March. While the Storm Prediction Center initially identified a low-probability severe threat, the environment was dominated by deep-layer moisture transport and training convective elements, leading to widespread 48-hour rainfall totals of 4 to 6 inches.

While the month began with an intensification on March 3rd that expanded D3 across counties like Carroll, Clinton, and Howard, a pattern of heavy rainfall triggered weekly improvements. By the March 31st update, Severe Drought (D2) and Extreme Drought (D3) had been completely removed from nearly all 17 previously affected counties.||This dramatic shift included the total elimination of D2/D3 conditions in a broad sub-region covering Warren, Vermillion, Fountain, Vigo, Parke, Montgomery, Boone, Clinton, Howard, Tipton, Hamilton, Madison, Delaware, Henry, and Randolph counties. By the end of the month, the only remaining vestiges of the winter drought were limited to the northern half of Carroll County and a small sliver of northern Tippecanoe County, which both remained in D2. In the eastern corridor, D3 conditions���which had been steady for months���were systematically trimmed back between March 10th and March 24th before finally being removed.||Precipitation throughout March was exceptionally high for these areas, with totals ranging from 4 to as much as 9 inches. Specifically, western counties like Warren and Fountain saw deluge amounts of 9 inches, while the central corridor from Vigo to Boone received 6 to 8.5 inches, providing the necessary moisture to end the drought status by mid-month. Even in the more stubborn drought areas of the northeast, such as Delaware and Howard counties, monthly totals of 4 to 5.5 inches neared or exceeded double the normal rainfall, finally allowing for the termination of severe drought conditions. The remaining counties in D2 would see improvements out of severe drought in early April.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: D2 conditions at the start of the month worsened to D3 on March 3rd before heavy rains trimmed the drought levels weekly until ending on the 17th. Rainfall amounts over the month were as much as 6 to 8 inches which allowed for the end of severe drought conditions.

Debris impacted an adjacent pole barn|with the pieces of metal being carried downstream into a yard|just to the east of the above noted intersection. The circulation|continued across mainly unplanted fields, but drone imagery|indicated a narrow area of very light scouring in the field and|inflow into the tornado. A tree fell onto SR 116 near E 300 S,|which a car ran into to. It then continued northeast before|lifting near the county line at S 700 W-1. Overall dry conditions that had peaked with widespread Extreme Drought (D3) in early March 2026 generally dissipated or significantly improved throughout the remainder of the month. While the month began with an intensification on March 3rd that expanded D3 across counties like Carroll, Clinton, and Howard, a pattern of heavy rainfall triggered weekly improvements. By the March 31st update, Severe Drought (D2) and Extreme Drought (D3) had been completely removed from nearly all 17 previously affected counties.||This dramatic shift included the total elimination of D2/D3 conditions in a broad sub-region covering Warren, Vermillion, Fountain, Vigo, Parke, Montgomery, Boone, Clinton, Howard, Tipton, Hamilton, Madison, Delaware, Henry, and Randolph counties. By the end of the month, the only remaining vestiges of the winter drought were limited to the northern half of Carroll County and a small sliver of northern Tippecanoe County, which both remained in D2. In the eastern corridor, D3 conditions���which had been steady for months���were systematically trimmed back between March 10th and March 24th before finally being removed.||Precipitation throughout March was exceptionally high for these areas, with totals ranging from 4 to as much as 9 inches. Specifically, western counties like Warren and Fountain saw deluge amounts of 9 inches, while the central corridor from Vigo to Boone received 6 to 8.5 inches, providing the necessary moisture to end the drought status by mid-month. Even in the more stubborn drought areas of the northeast, such as Delaware and Howard counties, monthly totals of 4 to 5.5 inches neared or exceeded double the normal rainfall, finally allowing for the termination of severe drought conditions. The remaining counties in D2 would see improvements out of severe drought in early April.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: D3 conditions at the start of the month for the entire county began to improve starting with the 17th issuance and weekly afterwards through the end of the month. D3 conditions ended on the March 24th issuance with D2 ending on the 31st. Rainfall amounts over the month were as much as 4 to 5 inches which allowed for the end of severe drought conditions.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful supercell thunderstorm tracked an EF-3 tornado across northern Newton and northwestern Jasper counties and another EF-1 tornado through northern Jasper County during the evening of March 10th. The EF-3 destroyed a number of homes and caused significant damage to many other homes, businesses, and infrastructure, especially in the town of Lake Village where two fatalities occurred as a result of the storm. Additional severe thunderstorms later in the evening brought one inch hail to northern Lake and Porter counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A destructive EF-3 tornado with estimated peak winds of 160 mph impacted portions of Newton and northwest Jasper Counties, most notably the community of Lake Village. After forming and causing EF-3 damage in Kankakee County, Illinois, this tornado crossed into Newton County between W 800 N Road and W 900 N Road near N 650 W Road. Upon entering the county, the tornado destroyed multiple outbuildings and significantly damaged multiple homes. On N 600 W Road, multiple homes were completely destroyed with debris blown clear of the foundations, consistent with EF-3 caliber winds. Nearby forested areas had almost all trees snapped or uprooted with some trees remaining standing with only stubs of a few large branches remaining, likely due to extensive lifted debris. Multiple homes were damaged, and a farm outbuilding was destroyed along N 500 W Road and along and near N 400 W Road. As the tornado crossed US-41 into the south side of Lake Village, it widened to approximately 1100 yards while damaging the roof and canopy of a gas station and a nearby retail building. Further north along N 300 W Road, multiple blocks of homes had significant roof damage and almost all trees were uprooted or snapped. The tornado continued eastward into a wooded area near the Lugene Links Golf Course, where a continuous corridor of trees was entirely uprooted. As the tornado neared W 950 N Road and N 150 W Road, a few homes were damaged, and a farm outbuilding was completely destroyed. The tornado continued to produce damage to trees and outbuildings as it traveled northeastward through mainly rural portions of northern Newton County and northern portions of Roselawn. The tornado continued into Jasper County and dissipated shortly thereafter. It was on the ground for over 35 miles and, at its peak, spanned a half mile in diameter. The storm destroyed numerous homes and resulted in around a dozen injuries and three fatalities: one in Kankakee County and the other two near Lake Village.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: In the wake of a cold front that produced widespread 60 mph wind gusts and severe thunderstorms, lake effect snow developed. Periods of significantly reduced visibilities were noted well inland across portions of La Porte, St. Joseph, and Elkhart Counties across northern Indiana due to the combination of snow and strong wind gusts. Storm total snowfall amount were generally in the 2 to 5 inch range across these locations with locally higher amount closer to 6 inches closer to the Indiana Michigan stateline.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The combination of periods of moderate to heavy lake effect snow and gusty winds of 30 to 40 mph led to significantly reduced visibilities at times along with slick road conditions. A CoCoRaHS observer 1.8 ENE of Granger reported 6.0 inches of snow. Outside of this specific location, snowfall amounts ranged from 2 to 4 inches. Numerous accidents and slide-offs were reported.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the late evening and overnight hours March 15th into March 16th, a strong upper level trough and associated cold front moved across the Ohio Valley. Ahead of the cold front, temperatures were in the 70s with dew point temperatures in the upper 50s and low 60s. This corridor of modest low-level destabilization contained between 250 and 500 J/kg of MLCAPE which was oriented immediately ahead of the surface front and the main line of showers and thunderstorms. With a corridor of 80 knot mid-level winds approaching from the west, effective bulk shear was between 40 and 50 knots for this event, creating a typical high-shear, low-CAPE setup for central Kentucky and southern Indiana. Given that the primary forcing mechanism was lifting along the cold front, convection evolved into a quasi-linear convective system that moved across southern Indiana during the late evening hours on March 15th into the early morning hours on March 16th. The main observed severe hazard was wind damage from straight-line winds, with scattered damage to trees and power lines being observed across southern Indiana. Brief mesovortices developed within the line of storms, prompting a tornado warning; however, no tornadoes were observed in southern Indiana during this event. The line of storms pushed east of the area by around 2 AM on March 16th, with much cooler air rushing into the area behind the cold front.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was down on Payne Koehler Road.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On March 13, 2026, a potent late-winter occluded storm system tracked across the Great Lakes while slowly filling, from early morning at 985 mb in northeastern Wisconsin, to late day at 989 mb over the northern Lower Peninsula of Michigan.  The system's cold front crossed northern and northeastern portions of central Indiana from 1000 to 1230EST.||Both an earlier corresponding low-level jet stream axis and a later tighter surface pressure gradient crossed the region, promoting widespread gusty winds veering from southwest to west-northwest while gusting to 45 to 57 mph.  When these two features briefly overlapped following the frontal passage, through midday to early afternoon hours, and also coupled with increased boundary layer mixing under plentiful sun, isolated highest wind gusts reached 58-67 mph.  Winds subsided quickly through evening hours.||This unusually intense gradient wind episode for the central Indiana region included measured gusts of 58+ mph at seven reporting stations;  four reports from Tipton County to Delaware County of semi trucks traveling on north-south roads being blown over to the east;  and widely scattered tree, power line, and minor property (mainly roof) damage that was most prevalent in Delaware County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A non-thunderstorm wind gust measured 58 mph from due west at 1054EST by KLAF Purdue University Airport.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the evening of March 22, 2026, an upper-level disturbance and an associated cold front swept across Central Indiana, triggering a broad swath of severe thunderstorms. Convection first initiated in the northern portions of the IND CWA, with the first reports of quarter-sized hail occurring in Howard and Madison counties. As the evening progressed, these storms moved into an environment characterized by moderate instability and strong vertical wind shear, allowing cells to become highly organized. The activity eventually evolved into a mixture of discrete supercells and organized line segments that tracked southeastward through the Indianapolis metro area and into southern Indiana.||The primary hazards associated with this event were large hail and damaging straight-line winds. The most significant hail report occurred in Knox County near Bicknell, where stones up to 2.00 inches in diameter were observed. Widespread hail ranging from 1.25 to 1.75 inches was also reported across Randolph, Marion, Sullivan, Daviess, and Martin counties. As the storms transitioned into a more linear configuration, wind damage became more prevalent. A peak measured gust of 64 mph was recorded in Jackson County, while a 62 mph gust was measured in Monroe County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorm wind gusts up to 35 mph were also estimated at this location.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the afternoon of March 15, 2026, a strong and deepening upper-level trough strengthened an already potent 990 mb surface low as it crossed the northwestern Midwest into the southern Great Lakes.  The resultant surface gradient over central Indiana produced non-thunderstorm wind gusts that caused tree, powerline, and/or power pole damage in 10 local counties. Some structural damage was also reported and a 59 mph non-thunderstorm gust was measured at the Shelbyville Airport ASOS.   ||A few hours later, during the 15th evening, a fast-moving quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) then swept across central Indiana ahead of a cold front, fueled by a potent 55-knot low-level jet and strong synoptic forcing. Despite modest instability, a high-shear environment allowed the line to maintain intensity as it tracked from Knox County at o Henry County. The Storm Prediction Center had placed the region under a Slight Risk, citing the potential for damaging straight-line winds. This was realized as a peak gust of 71 mph (62 knots) was measured in Marion County, while the Indianapolis International Airport (KIND) recorded a 58 mph gust.||The resulting damage was widespread, primarily affecting timber and utility infrastructure. A significant swath of downed trees and power lines stretched from Manilla to Arlington in Rush County. Structural impacts were also noted, including shingle damage in Madison County and a fence destroyed in Johnson County. Throughout the event, multiple state roads���including SR 32 and SR 45���were obstructed by fallen trees, and large pine trees up to 1.5 feet in diameter were snapped in Bartholomew County, reflecting the intensity of the straight-line winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 59 mph thunderstorm wind gust was measured at this location.

Some structural damage was also reported and a 59 mph non-thunderstorm gust was measured at the Shelbyville Airport ASOS.   ||A few hours later, during the 15th evening, a fast-moving quasi-linear convective system (QLCS) then swept across central Indiana ahead of a cold front, fueled by a potent 55-knot low-level jet and strong synoptic forcing. Despite modest instability, a high-shear environment allowed the line to maintain intensity as it tracked from Knox County at o Henry County. The Storm Prediction Center had placed the region under a Slight Risk, citing the potential for damaging straight-line winds. This was realized as a peak gust of 71 mph (62 knots) was measured in Marion County, while the Indianapolis International Airport (KIND) recorded a 58 mph gust.||The resulting damage was widespread, primarily affecting timber and utility infrastructure. A significant swath of downed trees and power lines stretched from Manilla to Arlington in Rush County. Structural impacts were also noted, including shingle damage in Madison County and a fence destroyed in Johnson County. Throughout the event, multiple state roads���including SR 32 and SR 45���were obstructed by fallen trees, and large pine trees up to 1.5 feet in diameter were snapped in Bartholomew County, reflecting the intensity of the straight-line winds.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was downed by thunderstorm wind gusts.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the evening of March 3, 2026, central Indiana experienced a wave of isolated severe weather fueled by record-breaking warmth and high humidity. The most significant severe report occurred in Hendricks County, where intense storms dropped 1 inch hail that was thick enough to completely cover road surfaces in areas like Avon. While the storms were scattered, they packed enough punch to create hazardous driving conditions and frequent cloud-to-ground lightning across the Interstate 74 corridor.||In addition to the hail, heavy rainfall led to localized flash flooding that caused significant disruptions in the southern suburbs. Near New Whiteland, rapid water accumulation forced the closure of several roads and led to a dangerous situation where a vehicle became stranded in floodwaters. This evening of activity was a precursor to a larger regional flooding event, as the 2 to 4 inches of rain saturated the ground and caused several local rivers to rise rapidly toward flood stage over the following 24 hours.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A large volume of hail which covered the roadways.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the evening of March 22, 2026, an upper-level disturbance and an associated cold front swept across Central Indiana, triggering a broad swath of severe thunderstorms. Convection first initiated in the northern portions of the IND CWA, with the first reports of quarter-sized hail occurring in Howard and Madison counties. As the evening progressed, these storms moved into an environment characterized by moderate instability and strong vertical wind shear, allowing cells to become highly organized. The activity eventually evolved into a mixture of discrete supercells and organized line segments that tracked southeastward through the Indianapolis metro area and into southern Indiana.||The primary hazards associated with this event were large hail and damaging straight-line winds. The most significant hail report occurred in Knox County near Bicknell, where stones up to 2.00 inches in diameter were observed. Widespread hail ranging from 1.25 to 1.75 inches was also reported across Randolph, Marion, Sullivan, Daviess, and Martin counties. As the storms transitioned into a more linear configuration, wind damage became more prevalent. A peak measured gust of 64 mph was recorded in Jackson County, while a 62 mph gust was measured in Monroe County.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Between the evening of March 3 and the late hours of March 4, 2026, a significant hydrologic event unfolded across central Indiana as a stalled frontal boundary interacted with a highly anomalous moisture profile. Driven by a robust 50-knot low-level jet, precipitable water values surged to nearly 1.30 inches���well above the 90th percentile for early March. While the Storm Prediction Center initially identified a low-probability severe threat, the environment was dominated by deep-layer moisture transport and training convective elements, leading to widespread 48-hour rainfall totals of 4 to 6 inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy rains washed out a bridge on County Road 1100 North at Wolf Creek.

On March 26, 2026, a potent cold front tracked across central Indiana, interacting with a warm and unstable airmass to trigger severe storms.  Severe thunderstorms developed rapidly, producing large hail and damaging wind gusts across northern central Indiana that downed trees and power lines, leading to over 1,700 power outages as residents dealt with the abrupt onset of hazardous weather.||Significant structural damage was observed, including a destroyed pole barn and a garage roof failure in Clinton County. While the environment supported supercellular rotation and prompted numerous tornado warnings, the only severe modes were straight-line damaging winds and large hail, with reports of 1.5-inch hail in Veedersburg. The convective activity gradually weakened as it progressed south of the I-70 corridor and encountered a more stable airmass, effectively concluding the active weather event for the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A 60 mph thunderstorm wind gust was measured at the KFKR AWOS.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A powerful supercell thunderstorm tracked an EF-3 tornado across northern Newton and northwestern Jasper counties and another EF-1 tornado through northern Jasper County during the evening of March 10th. The EF-3 destroyed a number of homes and caused significant damage to many other homes, businesses, and infrastructure, especially in the town of Lake Village where two fatalities occurred as a result of the storm. Additional severe thunderstorms later in the evening brought one inch hail to northern Lake and Porter counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An EF-1 tornado with estimated peak winds of 110 mph tracked across northern Jasper County south of Stoutsburg, Wheatfield, and Dunns Bridge. This tornado began about 2 miles south of Stoutsburg along CR W 1000 N, where there was damage noted to a solar panel field and power poles. The tornado moved east-northeast, causing damage to a farmstead on CR N 200 W. The most significant damage from this tornado was noted just south of Wheatfield on the 0-100 block of CR W 1100 N and on the 1100 block of State Route 49, where numerous homes sustained considerable damage and numerous trees and power poles were downed. The tornado continued to damage solar panel fields, trees, power poles, and farmsteads as it moved toward the Starke County line, passing through the unincorporated community of Tefft. The tornado dissipated before reaching Starke County on the 500 block of CR E 1350 N. Three minor injuries were reported with the tornado.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the late evening and overnight hours March 15th into March 16th, a strong upper level trough and associated cold front moved across the Ohio Valley. Ahead of the cold front, temperatures were in the 70s with dew point temperatures in the upper 50s and low 60s. This corridor of modest low-level destabilization contained between 250 and 500 J/kg of MLCAPE which was oriented immediately ahead of the surface front and the main line of showers and thunderstorms. With a corridor of 80 knot mid-level winds approaching from the west, effective bulk shear was between 40 and 50 knots for this event, creating a typical high-shear, low-CAPE setup for central Kentucky and southern Indiana. Given that the primary forcing mechanism was lifting along the cold front, convection evolved into a quasi-linear convective system that moved across southern Indiana during the late evening hours on March 15th into the early morning hours on March 16th. The main observed severe hazard was wind damage from straight-line winds, with scattered damage to trees and power lines being observed across southern Indiana. Brief mesovortices developed within the line of storms, prompting a tornado warning; however, no tornadoes were observed in southern Indiana during this event. The line of storms pushed east of the area by around 2 AM on March 16th, with much cooler air rushing into the area behind the cold front.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: There was a power pole and tree down and on fire on the 1100 block of Ridgewood Drive.

During the late evening and overnight hours March 15th into March 16th, a strong upper level trough and associated cold front moved across the Ohio Valley. Ahead of the cold front, temperatures were in the 70s with dew point temperatures in the upper 50s and low 60s. This corridor of modest low-level destabilization contained between 250 and 500 J/kg of MLCAPE which was oriented immediately ahead of the surface front and the main line of showers and thunderstorms. With a corridor of 80 knot mid-level winds approaching from the west, effective bulk shear was between 40 and 50 knots for this event, creating a typical high-shear, low-CAPE setup for central Kentucky and southern Indiana. Given that the primary forcing mechanism was lifting along the cold front, convection evolved into a quasi-linear convective system that moved across southern Indiana during the late evening hours on March 15th into the early morning hours on March 16th. The main observed severe hazard was wind damage from straight-line winds, with scattered damage to trees and power lines being observed across southern Indiana. Brief mesovortices developed within the line of storms, prompting a tornado warning; however, no tornadoes were observed in southern Indiana during this event. The line of storms pushed east of the area by around 2 AM on March 16th, with much cooler air rushing into the area behind the cold front.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A tree was blocking both lanes on the 7800 block of South 600 East.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the mid-to-late evening hours on March 22nd, a strong cold front dropped across the Ohio Valley, bringing a sharp drop in temperatures in addition to isolated strong to severe thunderstorms. During the afternoon hours, temperatures surged to near record levels in the mid-to-upper 80s, though dewpoint temperatures remained in the low-to-mid 50s. As a result, as the front moved into the region, instability remained relatively limited, with 500-1000 J/kg mixed-layer CAPE present. The large dewpoint depressions did allow for unseasonably high amounts of downdraft CAPE, and a strong gust front combined with the cold front to produce 45-55 mph winds separate from thunderstorms across southern Indiana and northern Kentucky. Scattered cells did become strong enough to produce near-severe size hail across southern Indiana, with between half inch and quarter size hail reported across Orange, Washington, and Harrison County.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Nickel to quarter size hail was observed in the eastern part of Orange County, near the Rego community. In French Lick and Paoli, smaller hailstones covered the ground.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the late evening and overnight hours March 15th into March 16th, a strong upper level trough and associated cold front moved across the Ohio Valley. Ahead of the cold front, temperatures were in the 70s with dew point temperatures in the upper 50s and low 60s. This corridor of modest low-level destabilization contained between 250 and 500 J/kg of MLCAPE which was oriented immediately ahead of the surface front and the main line of showers and thunderstorms. With a corridor of 80 knot mid-level winds approaching from the west, effective bulk shear was between 40 and 50 knots for this event, creating a typical high-shear, low-CAPE setup for central Kentucky and southern Indiana. Given that the primary forcing mechanism was lifting along the cold front, convection evolved into a quasi-linear convective system that moved across southern Indiana during the late evening hours on March 15th into the early morning hours on March 16th. The main observed severe hazard was wind damage from straight-line winds, with scattered damage to trees and power lines being observed across southern Indiana. Brief mesovortices developed within the line of storms, prompting a tornado warning; however, no tornadoes were observed in southern Indiana during this event. The line of storms pushed east of the area by around 2 AM on March 16th, with much cooler air rushing into the area behind the cold front.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Scottsburg Water Department had its roof peeled back on the 700 block of West Lake Road West.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During March 3 to March 7, 2026, large surface high pressure from the southeastern United States into the Atlantic focused a broad fetch of Gulf moisture northward into the Midwest.  A quasi-stationary frontal boundary near the Ohio Valley provided lift and focused, at times heavy rainfall over much of central Indiana, especially along the valley of the East Fork White River, and its tributaries northeast of Columbus through east-central central Indiana.||From the morning of the 3rd through dawn on the 4th, heavy rainfall over the watershed of the East Fork White's headwaters totaled mainly 2.00-3.75 inches.  Additional 1-day rainfall to dawn on the 5th, along the river's main stem from Columbus down through Martin County totaled generally 1.50-3.00 inches.  Further 2.5-day rainfall through late on the 7th was generally 1.00-2.00 inches along this main stem.  Overall 4.5-day rainfall totals were 4.00 to 6.00 inches for most portions of the entire East Fork White watershed.||Resultant widespread significant river flooding, including adjacent lowlands, from the Columbus area downstream through Jackson County, Lawrence County, and Martin County necessitated multiple water rescues.   Four persons over three counties perished when swept away by flood waters from the 6th to the 9th - three in motor vehicles and one in an airboat that encountered mechanical failure.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: The East Fork White River, while cresting in moderate flood stage in southeastern Lawrence County, swept away a truck carrying two people during the overnight early on the 9th.  Both occupants were found submerged in 8 feet of water west of the Tunnelton community near the intersection of Earl Road and Lawrenceport Road.

A strengthening storm system lifted through the Middle Mississippi Valley on the 19th, dragging its warm frontal zone northward through the Midwest, and bringing near-record high temperatures and anomalous dewpoints into central Indiana.  Multiple rounds of severe weather occurred over the region, from early morning large hail in two far-northern zones, covering roads in Warren County, to more organized evening severe weather from rotating supercell thunderstorms.  Through the evening of the 19th, the destabilized atmosphere combined with a stregthening low-level jet stream that progressed eastward into the region, boosting 0-1 km wind shear as high as 300 m2/s2.  A resultant cluster of discrete late-day to evening supercells were focused along the frontal zone, near or south of the Interstate 70 corridor, and produced scattered large hail over 6 counties and isolated wind damage to trees and/or power poles in 4 counties.  ||A stronger supercell with a history of producing two weak tornadoes in Crawford County, Illinois, continued into central Indiana, spawning an EF-0 tornado in Sullivan County, an intense EF-2 just west of Bloomington that caused extensive structural damage to homes, apartments, and airport facilities, and a brief EF-U in Decatur County;  this cell also produced ping-pong ball (1.50-inch diameter) sized hail in Greene and Monroe Counties.

The severe to extreme drought conditions that became entrenched across central Indiana during the winter of 2025-2026 persisted through the month of February. While January had seen a significant degradation and expansion of drought intensity, February was characterized by a stagnant status quo, where meager precipitation totals prevented any meaningful recovery. Extreme Drought (D3) remained fixed across the north-central corridor, while Severe Drought (D2) continued to blanket much of the surrounding West Central and Central Indiana counties.||The most intense conditions remained centered on Howard County, which stayed entirely within D3 intensity throughout the month. This Extreme Drought also maintained its grip on much of Carroll and Delaware counties, the northern half of Tipton County, and the northern third of Madison County. Furthermore, D3 conditions remained fixed in the far northwestern corner of Randolph County and northeastern Clinton County. Surrounding these areas, D2 conditions were maintained across the entirety of Warren, Tippecanoe, Fountain, and Vermillion counties, as well as the majority of Boone, Hamilton, and Montgomery counties. On the southern fringe of the drought���s extent, D2 intensity persisted in northwestern Parke, northwestern Vigo, and northern Henry counties.||Precipitation throughout February was once again critically low, frequently falling well below 50% of monthly norms. The driest conditions were observed in the northwest, where Warren County recorded less than a tenth of an inch of liquid equivalent, and Tippecanoe County saw only around 0.20 inches. Other hard-hit areas, including Carroll, Howard, and Delaware counties, saw totals struggle to reach 1.00 inch. While southern and eastern fringes like Henry and Parke counties received slightly higher totals ranging from 1.50 to 2.00 inches, the moisture was insufficient to overcome the long-term deficits. While D2 conditions were proscribed to end in March for several counties���including Vigo, Hamilton, and Boone���the drought remained firmly established for the majority of the region as the month concluded.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Precipitation totaled only around 1.20 to 1.60 inches across the month of February. This maintained D2 conditions across northwestern Vigo county. D2 conditions would end with the March 10th drought monitor update.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deep upper trough reinforced by a series of short waves plunging arctic air through interior North America, maintained persistent anomalous cold over central Indiana through January 2026's final week and February 1st, which was enhanced by a deep snow pack over most zones.  The cold outbreak's final embedded short wave plunged the farthest south, from the Middle Mississippi Valley on January 31st to the Carolina coast on the 1st.  Associated arctic surface high pressure centered over the Louisiana Gulf coast early on the 1st, extended its amplified ridge axis back over Indiana and into southeastern Canada, amid a weak surface gradient.  Resultant clear skies and light winds prevailed over central Indiana's remnant 5-10 inch snow pack from the January 31st late evening through daybreak on the 1st.  Temperatures fell generally as low as -5 to -15F with widespread resultant wind chills of -5F to -27F over the majority of central Indiana, with criteria wind chills limited to only Putnam, Hancock and Shelby Counties.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: On the 1st pre-dawn to early morning, temperatures as low as -17F, and light winds sustained under 5 mph...resulted in extreme wind chills as low as -27F.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deep upper trough reinforced by a series of short waves plunging arctic air through interior North America, maintained persistent anomalous cold over central Indiana through January's final week, which was enhanced by a deep snow pack over most zones.  Temperatures from early on the 26th through the 31st most often ranged from negative single digits up to the teens to around 20 degrees, with isolated periods featuring minimum temperatures as low as -20 degrees, or maxmum temperatures as low as widespread single digits on the 26th.  Corresponding sustained winds were most often under 10 mph when resultant wind chills approached or exceeded the negative 20 degree criteria, although higher speeds of 10-20 mph occasionally occurred, especially on the 26th.  The only criteria temperature observation was in Randoph County on the morning of the 30th.||Criteria wind chills were most prevalent during both the 26th daytime and the 26-27th overnight, occurring in 22 of the region's 39 counties during both periods.  Extreme cold occurred again in 15 zones within the 28th's AM hours.  Further extreme cold was confined within the same four central to northeast central Indiana counties, during overnights of both the 28-29th and 29-30th;  although wind chill values just shy of criteria were scattered across mainly northern portions of central Indiana.  A final period of extreme cold occurred prior to dawn on February 1st in two counties.  Overall, 29 central Indiana counties observed extreme cold during at least one period, and 16 of these zones observed criteria on at least 3 periods, most often the 26th through the 28th.  Spatial distribution of extreme cold was most consistent over the region's north-central quadrant, while exhibiting a subtle trend from all west-central zones on the 26th to a few east-central zones thereafter.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: On the 26th daytime, temperatures were as low as -3F, while breezy winds were sustained up to around 10 mph...resulting in marginally extreme wind chills as low as -20F.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A deep upper trough reinforced by a series of short waves plunging arctic air through interior North America, maintained persistent anomalous cold over central Indiana through January's final week, which was enhanced by a deep snow pack over most zones.  Temperatures from early on the 26th through the 31st most often ranged from negative single digits up to the teens to around 20 degrees, with isolated periods featuring minimum temperatures as low as -20 degrees, or maxmum temperatures as low as widespread single digits on the 26th.  Corresponding sustained winds were most often under 10 mph when resultant wind chills approached or exceeded the negative 20 degree criteria, although higher speeds of 10-20 mph occasionally occurred, especially on the 26th.  The only criteria temperature observation was in Randoph County on the morning of the 30th.||Criteria wind chills were most prevalent during both the 26th daytime and the 26-27th overnight, occurring in 22 of the region's 39 counties during both periods.  Extreme cold occurred again in 15 zones within the 28th's AM hours.  Further extreme cold was confined within the same four central to northeast central Indiana counties, during overnights of both the 28-29th and 29-30th;  although wind chill values just shy of criteria were scattered across mainly northern portions of central Indiana.  A final period of extreme cold occurred prior to dawn on February 1st in two counties.  Overall, 29 central Indiana counties observed extreme cold during at least one period, and 16 of these zones observed criteria on at least 3 periods, most often the 26th through the 28th.  Spatial distribution of extreme cold was most consistent over the region's north-central quadrant, while exhibiting a subtle trend from all west-central zones on the 26th to a few east-central zones thereafter.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: On the 26th daytime, temperatures were as low as -3F, while breezy winds were sustained around 10-15 mph...resulting in marginally extreme wind chills as low as -21F.
